title: Infinite Sin, Infinite Punishment?
hook: Does sinning against an infinite God really deserve punishment without end?
tldr: Aquinas argued that sin against an infinite God is infinite and deserves infinite punishment. But God cannot be harmed by finite creatures, the logic produces absurd ethics, it erases degrees of sin, and it contradicts the Torah's proportional justice. Scripture's own language of 'until' and its promise of no more pain point to temporary, corrective punishment.
big_idea: Finite beings committing finite sins deserve finite, corrective consequences.

points.title: Limited knowledge breeds sin
points.text: Humanity holds a single fruit of all possible knowledge. Our limits make us fallible judges and actors, so we need grace from God, each other and ourselves.

points.title: The status argument
points.text: Aquinas: the graver the person offended, the graver the sin; striking a head of state is worse than a private citizen, so sin against infinite God earns infinite punishment.

points.title: God cannot be harmed
points.text: An infinite God is beyond harm or diminishment by human sin. Like a parent absorbing a toddler's tantrum, he can endure any offense without extreme retribution.

points.title: Justice is proportional
points.text: The Torah's 'eye for an eye' matches punishment to the offense, not the status of the offended. Equating God's nature with the offense is a category mistake.

points.title: Punishment 'until' the debt is paid
points.text: Jesus spoke of prisoners held until they repay everything. 'Until' implies a set duration, an end once the debt is paid.

points.title: Grace increased all the more
points.text: Endless torment clashes with a God who will not break a bruised reed and promises an end to pain. Temporary punishment upholds justice and points to restoration.

sections.summary: A naive couple, deceived by the Serpent's promise that they could be all-knowing like God, ate from the Tree of Knowledge. Humanity gained more knowledge than any species, yet compared to all knowledge, like all the world's fruits and vegetables, we hold one piece of fruit. God's claim to omniscience is not arrogant because it is true; human claims to full understanding only expose our limits.

The gap between our knowledge and all that can be known is fertile ground for sin. Even an astute judge errs when missing crucial facts; ordinary people judge harshly without the full picture. God is the ideal judge. Humans, probably including Adam and Eve, decide under limits of time and knowledge, worsened by stress, physical conditions and emotional bias. The cry 'it's not fair' exposes the gap between perception and reality.

sections.h: Jesus the exception, grace the response
sections.summary: Jesus is the exception to human imperfection: a living example and perfect standard rather than a detailed manual. Striving to be Christlike lessens sin's effects, but life still demands knowledge we lack. Perfection is unattainable in this world, and recognizing that tempts us to judge ourselves and others harshly. Instead, limited, fallible humans need patience, understanding and forgiveness from God, from each other and from themselves.

sections.h: Should an Infinite God Infinitely Punish His Finite-Created Humans?
sections.summary: A sophisticated argument for eternal punishment says finite, emotional, limited humans commit infinite sins because they offend an infinite being. It draws on the intuition that an offense grows with the dignity of the one offended: slapping a child is less severe than slapping the king's son. Thomas Aquinas, a 13th-century Dominican friar, put it in the Summa Theologiae: striking a head of state is worse than a private citizen, and God is infinitely great.

sections.h: Flaws one and two: no harm, absurd ethics
sections.summary: First, infinite God cannot be hurt or diminished by human sin, so infinite consequences are disproportionate; like a parent absorbing a tantrum, God's love endures everything and his justice corrects. If anything, his dignity is injured by those teaching eternal conscious torment. Second, the logic makes cursing a prime minister or pastor worse than torturing a dog or cursing a layman, ranking status over real harm, a framework of class and status.

sections.h: Flaws three and four: moral absolutism, finite sins
sections.summary: If finite beings can merit infinite punishment, any small deviation from perfection deserves the most extreme penalty, an unjust absolutism ignoring intention and nuance. Finite humans cannot commit infinite sins; if the soul is infinite, even killing only briefly interrupts physical life. Making every sin infinite erases distinctions, equating a white lie about a wedding dress with ISIS and Hamas raping or killing children, though Scripture differentiates sins.

sections.h: Flaw five: proportional justice in the Torah
sections.summary: God's law is proportional, following lex talionis, an eye for an eye. Finite actions deserve finite consequences regardless of who is offended; tying punishment to the offended party's nature is a Category Mistake Fallacy. Picture a father threatening to set his child on fire for imperfection, or a judge giving 75 years to a poor 18-year-old single mother who stole baby food from Walmart rather than a small grocery store.

sections.h: Flaws six and seven: infinity and the purpose of punishment
sections.summary: Infinity is not merely 'bigger' but a different kind of concept, absent from Israel's Law; when Israel sinned against God, consequences were always finite. Punishment is by definition temporary and corrective, so infinite punishment is self-contradictory, purposeless suffering offering no learning or repentance, mere vengeance. Methodist minister Arthur P. Adams (1848-1920) wrote that kolasis aims at reformation, so 'endless punishment' is nonsense, like endless correction.

The theory has no scriptural support. Job's 'Three Stooges', Eliphaz, Zophar and Bildad, argue similarly, and Elihu challenges them: if you sin, how does that affect God? Your wickedness only affects humans like yourself. When God speaks, he condemns the three friends but does not rebuke Elihu, suggesting Elihu's view of divine justice was right. The infinite-punishment argument is illogical, misreads infinity and portrays God badly.

sections.h: Why Only a Temporary Punishment Makes Sense
sections.summary: Imagine, distracted while driving, you accidentally kill a baby who goes to eternal paradise. Should you be tormented forever in a fiery furnace? Of course not. If destinations converge in one eternal state, even the gravest misfortunes here are temporary. If God hates sin but loves sinners, his justice should eradicate sin's effects, not sinners. God's image remains even in the depraved, so torturing sinners forever tortures his own image.

sections.h: What Purpose Could Eternal Torment Serve?
sections.summary: The Augustinian-Calvinist hell of endless torture is neither corrective nor rehabilitative and offers no chance to change. It mirrors immature human vengeance, not the loving, forgiving, compassionate God of the Bible whose justice restores. Jesus' metaphors of a debtor delivered to torturers until he repays everything, or not emerging until the last pittance is paid, imply a set duration that ends when the debt is paid.

The justice paradigm says all humanity merits perpetual burning. But temporal sins with temporary effects deserve temporary punishments; otherwise punishment is sadistic retribution. The prophets show a gentle parent who will not break a bruised reed. Revelation promises an end to death, mourning and pain; with eternal hellfire, would God erase memories of unsaved loved ones and our identities? Temporary punishment shows grace abounding more than sin, aiming at restoring all things.

children.label: Logic
children.note: The argument breaks on its own terms.

children.label: God cannot be harmed
children.note: Finite acts barely affect an infinite God; he can absorb any offense.

children.label: Infinity misunderstood
children.note: Infinity is a different kind of concept, not just 'bigger'.

children.label: Category mistake
children.note: Confuses the nature of the being with the nature of the offense.

children.label: Status over harm
children.note: Cursing a pastor becomes worse than torturing a dog.

children.label: Moral absolutism
children.note: Any tiny flaw earns the most extreme punishment possible.

children.label: All sins equal
children.note: A white lie equals murdering children, against John 19:11.

children.label: Scripture
children.note: The Bible does not support it.

children.label: Eye for an eye
children.note: Torah justice is proportional to the offense.

children.label: Elihu unrebuked
children.note: Our sin does not affect God; his friends are condemned.

children.label: Until the debt is paid
children.note: Jesus' prison metaphors imply punishment ends.

visuals.title: Weighing the crime against the sentence
visuals.caption: Proportional justice matches punishment to the offense, not to the status of the one offended.

right.label: Infinite torment
items: Same for white lies and murder

visuals.title: Elihu's answer to the friends
visuals.text: I would like to reply to you [Job] and to your friends with you (Eliphaz, Zophar, and Bildad]. Look up at the heavens and see; gaze at the clouds so high above you. If you sin, how does that affect him? If your sins are many, what does that do to him? ... Your wickedness only affects humans like yourself.

notes.note: Job's friends voice an argument like Aquinas'; God later condemns them.

notes.phrase: If you sin, how does that affect him?
notes.note: An infinite God cannot be harmed or diminished by finite human sin.

notes.phrase: Your wickedness only affects humans like yourself
notes.note: Sin's real damage is to people, so justice should address harm, not status. God never rebukes Elihu.

mythfact.myth: A sin's seriousness depends on how important the offended person is.
mythfact.fact: Taken seriously, that makes cursing a prime minister worse than torturing a dog; biblical justice weighs harm and proportion, not status.

mythfact.myth: Infinite punishment is just because God is infinite.
mythfact.fact: Finite beings cannot commit infinite sins; the Torah's eye-for-an-eye justice is proportional, and Israel's sins against God always had finite consequences.

mythfact.myth: Endless punishment still serves a purpose.
mythfact.fact: Punishment corrects, deters or rehabilitates; endless punishment allows no learning or repentance, making it purposeless vengeance.

terms.meaning: The principle of 'an eye for an eye': proportional justice matching punishment to the offense.
Confusing the nature of the offended being with the nature of the offense to justify infinite punishment.
Greek word translated 'punishment', whose purpose, Arthur P. Adams argued, is the reformation of the offender.
The view that all sinners, hence all humanity, merit perpetual burning in hellfire.

quotes.text: Now a sin that is against God is infinite; the higher the person against whom it is committed, the graver the sin
now to talk about endless “punishment”, is nonsense, as much as it would be to talk of endless correction, or endless reforming.
the punishment should be proportionate to the crime, not to the status of the offended party.

verses.role: Elihu: our sin cannot affect God; God does not rebuke him.
Eye for an eye: God's own law demands proportional justice.
Scripture distinguishes degrees of sin, which infinite punishment would erase.
Delivered to torturers until he repays everything: punishment with an end point.
Not emerging until the last pittance is paid implies a set duration.
Parallel to Matthew 5:26: release once the debt is paid.
God does not break a bruised reed: a gentle, reforming parent.
Promise that pain and mourning cease, impossible if eternal hellfire exists.
Where sin increased, grace increased more; temporary punishment honors this.

quiz.q: Who articulated the argument that sin against infinite God deserves infinite punishment in the Summa Theologiae?
quiz.why: The 13th-century Dominican friar Thomas Aquinas compared it to striking a head of state rather than a private citizen.

quiz.q: What happens when God speaks at the end of Job?
options: He condemns Eliphaz, Zophar and Bildad but not Elihu
quiz.why: God's silence on Elihu, who said our sin does not affect God, suggests Elihu's view of justice was right.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' word 'until' in his prison metaphors imply?
options: Punishment ends once the debt is paid
quiz.why: 'Until he should repay everything' implies a set duration rather than eternal torment.

reflect: Should the severity of a wrong depend on who is offended, or on the harm actually done?
